summary: LLZ specialization-image and basis-covariance checkpoint. Gives declaration-level proofs for simultaneous evaluation constraints, determinant ideals, exact coordinate images and polynomial witnesses, plus logarithmic-matrix coordinate algebra, integral shear choices and denominator-qualified quadratic Euler formulas. The actual crystalline regulator, Wach/Mellin/Iwasawa instantiations, integral image theorem and de Rham extension remain explicit work; neither stage is closed.

conventions.cyclotomic: The LLZ source assumes odd p, uses HT(Q_p(1))=+1 and separates G=Delta times Gamma_1. R=Lambda_E(Gamma_1)=O_E[[X]][1/varpi], X=gamma-1, has bounded coefficients. It is not all of E[[X]]. The generic algebraic statements do not silently assume the source arithmetic hypotheses have been proved.
conventions.evaluation: Evaluation context: E is a field; R is a nonzero commutative E-algebra which is a domain; d,m are natural numbers; x:Fin m to E is injective; t is in R; ev_j:R to E are E-algebra homomorphisms with ev_j(t)=x_j. Each q_j=t-algebraMap(x_j) is NONZERO, and ev_j(f)=0 iff q_j divides f. J is a finite set of evaluation indices; V_j is an E-subspace of E^d. For the analytic application x_j belongs to the maximal ideal. Distinctness, the domain hypothesis and nonzero q_j are substantive, separate requirements.
conventions.matrices: Vectors of coefficients are rows; vectors of basis elements are columns. Domain basis n'=Un changes coordinates by U inverse. M maps bounded coordinates to analytic coordinates and changes by U M B inverse when the target basis changes by B. Apply the coefficient homomorphism to U where its ring differs from that of M.
conventions.determinants: Equality of principal determinant ideals is represented by association of nonzero generators; a basis does not choose a canonical scalar normalization.
conventions.integral: A nonzero determinant over O is not necessarily a unit. Constant O-integral basis changes preserve lattices. Finite-index integral image is weaker than surjectivity and rational surjectivity is weaker still.

nodes.title: Quadratic Frobenius inverse
nodes.statement: Define P(a,b,Phi)=-b^(-1)(Phi+aI) as an explicit matrix expression. It is an inverse only under the separately stated quadratic relation and b nonzero.
hypotheses: E is a field; Phi is a finite square matrix.
proofSteps: Use scalar multiplication and the existing matrix identity; no matrix inverse is used in the definition.
acceptance: Keep the nonzero-b hypothesis in the inverse theorem, not as an implicit convention about total inverses.

uses.how: Replace an inverse of Frobenius by a guarded polynomial formula.

nodes.title: Frobenius inverse identities
nodes.statement: If Phi^2+aPhi+bI=0 and b is nonzero, then Phi P=P Phi=I.
hypotheses: E is a field; Phi is a d by d matrix; Phi^2+aPhi+bI=0; b is nonzero.
proofSteps: Expand Phi P using the quadratic relation to obtain -b^(-1)(-bI)=I.
P is a polynomial in Phi, so the expansion on the other side is identical.
acceptance: Prove both sides without assuming commutativity of the full matrix ring.

nodes.title: Quadratic Euler inverse
nodes.statement: Define Q(a,b,Phi)=(1+a+b)^(-1)(Phi+(1+a)I). This is the inverse candidate for I-Phi, not an unqualified inverse at singular Euler factors.
hypotheses: E is a field; Phi is a finite square matrix.
proofSteps: Form the indicated scalar multiple of a degree-one polynomial in Phi.
acceptance: Distinguish the denominator 1+a+b from the separate denominator b.

uses.how: Make the second excluded denominator explicit in Euler interpolation.

nodes.title: Euler inverse identities
nodes.statement: If Phi^2+aPhi+bI=0 and s=1+a+b is nonzero, then (I-Phi)Q=Q(I-Phi)=I.
hypotheses: E is a field; Phi is square; the quadratic relation holds; 1+a+b is nonzero.
proofSteps: Expand (I-Phi)(Phi+(1+a)I) and reduce Phi^2 using the quadratic relation; the answer is sI.
Divide only by s nonzero and repeat on the other side.
acceptance: Do not infer this statement when 1 is an eigenvalue of Phi.

sources.match: The source calculation becomes a typed two-sided inverse identity with its denominator hypothesis.

nodes.title: Quadratic Euler-operator formula
nodes.statement: Assume p,b and s=1+a+b are nonzero. With P=Phi^(-1) and Q=(I-Phi)^(-1) certified by the preceding lemmas, Q(I-p^(-1)P) equals [(1+a+pb)Phi+(a(1+a+pb)+b(p-1))I]/[pb(1+a+b)].
hypotheses: E is a field; Phi is a finite square matrix; Phi^2+aPhi+bI=0; p,b,1+a+b are nonzero.
proofSteps: Insert the two explicit polynomial expressions.
Reduce the quadratic term by Phi^2=-aPhi-bI, collect the coefficient of Phi and the scalar term, and use the three nonzero denominator hypotheses.
This is an algebraic input to interpolation, not an interpolation theorem or a definition on the excluded eigenspaces.
acceptance: Test Phi=2,a=-5,b=6,p=5, which gives -9/10; exclude Phi=1 and zero Frobenius where appropriate.

nodes.title: Specialization-constraint module
nodes.statement: For a finite set J of evaluation indices, define the R-submodule S_J(V) of R^d by F in S_J(V) iff ev_j(F) is in V_j for every j in J, with componentwise evaluation.
hypotheses: E is a field and R a commutative E-algebra; ev_j are E-algebra homomorphisms; V_j are E-subspaces. No domain, distinctness or divisibility assumption is needed just to define S.
proofSteps: Closure under R-scalar multiplication follows because ev_j(rF)=ev_j(r)ev_j(F) and V_j is an E-subspace. Addition and zero are componentwise.
acceptance: Retain the actual evaluation maps and the finite set of imposed conditions.

uses.how: The image module with finitely many specialization constraints.
The module against which the actual Coleman image must be compared.

nodes.title: Division by distinct evaluation factors
nodes.statement: In the evaluation context, ev_j(f)=0 for all j in J iff the product of q_j over J divides f. Repeated points are not allowed.
hypotheses: The evaluation context in conventions.evaluation, including injectivity of x and the evaluation-kernel divisibility hypotheses.
proofSteps: Induct on J. Divide by the newly extracted q_j using the kernel hypothesis.
At another point i, ev_i(q_j)=x_i-x_j is nonzero; hence the quotient still vanishes there. Apply the induction hypothesis.
The converse follows by evaluating the product.
acceptance: A repeated evaluation point does not imply a double zero.

sources.match: Makes explicit the distinct-factor divisibility used in the first image inclusion.

nodes.title: Single-condition basis
nodes.statement: For J={j}, S_J(V) has an R-basis with row matrix diag(1,...,1,q_j,...,q_j)C, where C is an E-basis of E^d adapted to V_j and q_j occurs codim(V_j) times. Its determinant is a nonzero E-scalar times q_j^codim(V_j).
hypotheses: The evaluation context, including R a domain and q_j nonzero.
proofSteps: Extend a basis of V_j to a basis of E^d using the existing vector-space basis extension.
In these coordinates, precisely the complementary coordinates must have ev_j=0. The kernel hypothesis divides them by q_j.
Multiplication by q_j is injective because R is a domain and q_j is nonzero; it identifies each complementary R-coordinate with q_j R.
The diagonal determinant and determinant of C give the determinant with its unit factor.
acceptance: Do not drop the domain or nonzero-factor assumptions; nonzero zero-divisors do not give free principal summands.

sources.match: Expands the adapted-basis and division argument of the source.

nodes.title: Invertibility at a new point
nodes.statement: Let B be a row-basis matrix for previous constraints with det(B)=epsilon times the product over i in J of q_i^n_i, epsilon a unit in R. If j is not in J, ev_j(B) is invertible over E.
hypotheses: The evaluation context; the stated determinant factorization; j not in J.
proofSteps: An algebra homomorphism sends epsilon to a unit.
Each evaluated q_i is x_j-x_i, nonzero by distinctness. Evaluate the determinant product to obtain a nonzero determinant.
Use the adjugate identity over E.
acceptance: The point must be distinct from all points whose factors occur in the determinant.

sources.match: This is the source's evaluated basis matrix at the new node.

nodes.title: Transported specialization subspace
nodes.statement: For an E-subspace V of E^d and a matrix C over E, define W={c:cC is in V}, a submodule preimage. If C is invertible, W=VC^(-1) in row-vector notation.
hypotheses: E is a field; C is square. Invertibility is required only for the inverse description and dimension comparison.
proofSteps: Use the existing linear row-multiplication map and Submodule.comap.
acceptance: Do not silently identify regulator-coordinate constraints with Coleman-coordinate constraints.

nodes.title: Basis for simultaneous constraints
nodes.statement: Construct an R-basis of S_J(V), indexed by Fin d, by successively imposing each evaluation condition. This extends the one-point construction and does not claim an integral basis for constraints over O_E.
hypotheses: The entire evaluation context, including R a domain, all q_j nonzero, distinct points and the principal evaluation kernels.
proofSteps: Start with the standard basis when J is empty.
At j not in J use constraintBasisEvaluationInvertible and replace V_j by transportedSpecialization(V_j,ev_j(B)).
Apply singleConstraintBasisExists to the coefficient module and multiply its row matrix C on the LEFT of B. The resulting rows form a basis of the new S.
Carry the determinant product in the same induction; this simultaneously supplies the invariant for the next step.
acceptance: There is no circular dependency on the final determinant theorem: the induction proves the basis and its determinant invariant together.

uses.how: Prove full R-rank and the determinant of the constrained image module.

nodes.title: Polynomial witness for the image generator
nodes.statement: In the evaluation context construct F in S_J(V) whose k-th coordinate is exactly g_k. Other coordinates can be chosen as polynomials in t with E-coefficients.
hypotheses: The entire evaluation context; k is a coordinate in Fin d.
proofSteps: At a point in J_k choose zero in V_j. Outside J_k choose v in V_j with v_k nonzero and multiply by ev_j(g_k)/v_k.
Interpolate each of the other coordinates with Lagrange.interpolate on J and substitute t. Set the k-th coordinate to g_k itself.
Evaluation at every node returns the chosen vector by the E-algebra property and Lagrange.eval_interpolate_at_node.
acceptance: This is a generator witness, not merely an inclusion or a dimension count; its coefficients need not be integral.

proofSteps: Compose the supplied map with the existing linear equivalence. Use standard coordinates, not a new regulator record.

proofSteps: Map each standard vector in R^d through e inverse, j and b.

nodes.title: Constant basis covariance
nodes.statement: With column basis vectors n'=Un and nu'=Bnu, U in GL_d(R), B in GL_d(A), the coordinate row changes by c'=cU inverse and the matrix by M'=algebraMap(U) M B inverse. Hence c'M'=cM B inverse, so the vector in Y is unchanged. Fixing the crystalline basis means B=I.
hypotheses: Actual coordinate bases and invertible matrices over their declared rings.
Lattice-preserving Wach application: U belongs to GL_d(O_E). A rational matrix only yields a rational comparison.
proofSteps: Expanding the same vector in the two domain bases gives c'U=c.
Apply j to n'=Un and substitute nu=B inverse times nu'.
Multiply associatively; do not interchange matrices.
For Wach modules invoke only the good-basis theorem and permitted constant integral transformations, not arbitrary power-series basis changes.
acceptance: Check both domain and target basis changes; the inverse on Coleman coordinates is essential.

nodes.title: Transformation of specialization lines
nodes.statement: Over a field, assume 1-e1e2 nonzero and (F',G')=(F,G)A. Then F=0 iff F'=e1G'; G=0 iff G'=e2F'; and F=rG iff (1+e2r)F'=(e1+r)G'. If e1+r and 1+e2r are nonzero, the latter line has both coordinate projections nonzero.
hypotheses: E is a field and 1-e1e2 is nonzero.
proofSteps: Expand each difference; it equals (1-e1e2) times the original difference.
Use the determinant's nonvanishing for both implications. Divide the transformed slope only when its denominator is nonzero.
acceptance: Treat both axes as well as finite nonzero slopes.

sources.match: Preserves all three cases of the source's change-of-lines argument.

nodes.title: Integral shear avoiding finitely many slopes
nodes.statement: Let O embed in a field E, with O a commutative local domain and its maximal ideal infinite. For finitely many nonzero slopes r_i in E, choose nonzero e1,e2 in that maximal ideal such that e1+r_i and 1+e2r_i are nonzero for every i. Then det A is a unit in O. Finite extensions of Q_p satisfy the infinite-ideal hypothesis via distinct positive powers of a uniformizer.
hypotheses: O is a commutative local domain; E is a field; O to E is injective; maximalIdeal(O) is infinite; the slope set is finite.
proofSteps: Avoid the finite set {0,-r_i} when choosing e1, using the injection O to E.
Avoid {0,-r_i inverse} when choosing e2.
Since e1e2 is in the maximal ideal, 1-e1e2 is a unit.
This repairs the insufficiency of merely requiring a nonzero determinant and does not need a large residue field.
acceptance: Uniformizer powers provide infinitely many choices even when the residue field is small.

nodes.title: Rational surjectivity after integral basis change
nodes.statement: In the two-dimensional evaluation context, suppose each V_j is a one-dimensional E-subspace of E^2. A constant integral shear chosen as above makes both projections of S_J(V)A equal to R. For R=O_E[[X]][1/varpi] this is rational surjectivity, not an assertion that integral Coleman images equal O_E[[X]].
hypotheses: The entire evaluation context with d=2 and dim_E V_j=1 for every imposed condition; O embeds in E and is as in integralShearChoice.
proofSteps: Each line is an axis or has a finite nonzero slope. Collect the finitely many slopes.
Use integralShearChoice and shearSpecializationLines; every transformed line has both projections nonzero.
Evaluation commutes with the constant matrix A, so S(V)A=S(VA). The two forced-zero sets are empty and coordinateImage_eq gives the conclusion.
Integral finite-index conclusions still need LLZ Theorem 5.10 and its integral lower inclusion, recorded as remaining work.
acceptance: The proper ideal (5,X) in Z_5[[X]] becomes the full ring after inverting 5; rational surjectivity does not remove the integral correction.
